author: BBC News
description:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
 
Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.
 
Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.
 
So what do you need to know about it? BBC lead weather presenter Simon King answers some of the top questions.

author: BBC News
description:
When the internet’s biggest fanfiction site disappears, there’s one thing you can still count on: a network of fans. 

AO3 hosts more than 18 million works, including many sexually explicit stories, and writing inspired by popular IP, such as Harry Potter, Twilight and Heated Rivalry. 

And the fans have been sharing “fics” on drives to keep each other going while their online haven is down. The non-profit behind AO3, announced the site would be offline for two to four weeks, citing a “security incident”. 

In this episode, Marianna and Matt discuss why people are panicking and whether after other cyber security threats recently - including PHP - the internet is becoming more fragile.

Plus - Marianna has done an experiment to test how AI chatbots might be influencing how people vote and how it could mean for future elections.

Tech shares on stock markets around the world fell steeply after the US midterm elections, prompted by fears that the Democrats would use their new political power to crack down on artificial intelligence. 

Several states elected senators, representatives and governors who have promised to rein in Big Tech and ban or regulate AI data centres. They have become a significant concern for American voters due to their energy usage and environmental impact. 

This is in stark contrast to President Donald Trump, who has championed AI, dubbing it "super intelligence". Trump has close ties to some of the tech bosses driving AI development, including Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. He recently said states "should want as many data centres" as they can get, because they generate "tremendous amounts of money".

description:
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.

description:
Preppers have long been planning for the worst-case scenario. Are governments now doing the same?  

The UK government has launched a national “Be Ready” campaign, urging people to keep enough food, water and medicine at home to prepare for three days of disruption.

Other European countries have similar policies. But for preppers, whose mission it is to ready themselves for a future disaster, this is old news. Have the preppers been vindicated? And what exactly are we prepping for?

Tristan Redman speaks to Lucy Easthope about her role as a disaster planning expert and Gabriel Gatehouse joins us in the studio to talk about what he's learnt from interviewing British preppers.

description:
An AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.
 
This happened during a BBC investigation into AI toys and it made the unprompted remark while being asked how babies are made.

AI toy company founder Paul Clarke said the industry was "crying out" for regulation - a call echoed by the children's commissioner for Wales.
 
The UK government said children's safety would always be a top priority and it supported innovation while ensuring products were safe.
 
Repeated efforts to find the makers of Doubao were unsuccessful, so the BBC was unable to ask the manufacturer why the teddy made this comment.
